options_en: In order to ensure that every detail reflected the heritage of
the family, the exquisite silk gown was especially designed
for the bride to wear on her wedding day.
No Error
options_hi: In order to ensure that every detail reflected the heritage of
the family, the exquisite silk gown was especially designed
for the bride to wear on her wedding day.

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B) Replace “especially” with “specially”

Rule / Concept: The "Specific Purpose" Rule

  • Specially: This adverb is used when an action is performed for a limited, specific purpose or for a particular person/occasion. It often modifies verbs like designed, made, created, organized, or trained. Think of it as "specifically for this one task."

  • Especially: This adverb is used to mean "particularly" or "above all others." It is used to single out something from a group or to intensify an adjective.

Application to the Given Question

"...the exquisite silk gown was especially designed for the bride..."

The sentence focuses on the purpose of the gown's creation. It wasn't just "particularly" designed; it was custom-designed for one specific person and one specific event. Whenever you are talking about a tailored service, a custom-built object, or a dedicated training program

Corrected Sentence In order to ensure that every detail reflected the heritage of the family, the exquisite silk gown was specially designed for the bride to wear on her wedding day

More Examples for Clarity

  • This car was specially modified for racing. (Specific purpose) ✅

  • I like all desserts, especially chocolate cake. (Singling out one from a group) ✅

  • The meeting was specially convened to discuss the crisis. (Specific reason) ✅

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: So arrogantly he dismisses the valid concerns of his colleagues
that the entire department has become increasingly
reluctant to collaborate on any future research initiatives.
No Error
options_hi: So arrogantly he dismisses the valid concerns of his colleagues
that the entire department has become increasingly
reluctant to collaborate on any future research initiatives.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (A) Replace “he dismisses” with “does he dismiss”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Inversion with "So + Adverb" (Manner)

When a sentence starts with "So + Adverb of Manner" (such as So rudely, So arrogantly, So beautifully), it is done to emphasize the manner in which an action is performed. In such cases, the sentence must follow the Partial Inversion structure.

This means an auxiliary verb (do, does, did) must be placed before the subject. If the original sentence is in the Simple Present tense and the subject is singular (like he), we use "does" and change the main verb to its base form

Application to the Given Question

So arrogantly he dismisses the valid concerns...

In this sentence, the phrase "So arrogantly" starts the sentence. The subject is "he" and the verb is "dismisses" (Simple Present). To apply inversion correctly, the auxiliary verb "does" must be placed before "he," and the verb "dismisses" must be changed to the base form "dismiss."

Corrected Sentence

So arrogantly does he dismiss the valid concerns of his colleagues that the entire department has become increasingly reluctant to collaborate on any future research initiatives.

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 ✅: So sweetly did she sing that everyone was mesmerized.

Example 2 ✅: So fluently does he speak French that people often mistake him for a local.

Example 3 ✅: So bitterly did they argue that the neighbors had to call the police.

🧠 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

  • The "That" Trigger: These sentences almost always follow the pattern: So + Adverb + Auxiliary + Subject + Main Verb... + THAT + Result.

  • Verb Form: A very common trap in SSC Mains is using "does" but forgetting to remove the 's' from the main verb (e.g., So rudely does he behaves ❌). Always use the base form.

  • Tense Harmony: Ensure the auxiliary verb matches the tense of the result clause. If the result is "wants" (present), use "does/do." If the result is "wanted" (past), use "did."

📌 Rule / Concept: Elicit vs. Illicit

Elicit (Verb): To draw out, evoke, or provoke a reaction, response, or information from someone. (e.g., "The comedian elicited a roar of laughter.")

Illicit (Adjective): Forbidden by law, rules, or custom; illegal or unauthorized. (e.g., "The businessman was involved in illicit activities.")

💢 Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the word is used as a verb following the infinitive "to." The context is about "drawing out" or "evoking" an emotion (interest) from the students. Therefore, the spelling elicit is perfectly correct. Had the sentence used "illicit," it would have been an error because "illicit interest" would imply an illegal interest, which does not fit the context of a classroom.

More Examples for Clarity -

Example 1: The questionnaire was designed to elicit honest feedback. Example 2: He was arrested for the illicit sale of narcotics. Example 3: A good teacher knows how to elicit the best from her students.

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: The project manager will not authorize the
disbursement of funds unless the contractor
will submit the audited expenditure reports.
No Error
options_hi: The project manager will not authorize the
disbursement of funds unless the contractor
will submit the audited expenditure reports.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (C).

Replace “will submit” with “submits”.

📌 Rule/Concept: The "No Will" Rule in Conditional Clauses

Don’t use future tense with these conjunctions- when, while, if, until, unless, provided that, as soon as, before, after, etc.

Always write the condition part in simple future tense.

In a Type 1 Conditional sentence (expressing a probable future), the sentence is divided into two parts: the Conditional Clause (starting with if, unless, until, as soon as, when) and the Main Clause.

Using "will" or "shall" in both clauses is a "Double Future" error. Even though the condition refers to the future, the grammar requires the Simple Present to express it.

💢 Application to the Given Question - The word unless introduces a conditional clause. According to the rule, you cannot use "will" in a clause starting with "unless." Since the subject "the contractor" is singular, we must use the Simple Present verb submits. The main clause ("The project manager will not authorize") correctly uses the future tense, so the error lies solely in the conditional part.

More Examples for Clarity -

Example 1 ✅: If it rains, we will cancel the match. (Not: If it will rain)

Example 2 ✅: Until the sun sets, we will not return home. (Not: Until the sun will set)

Example 3 ✅: When she arrives, I will inform you. (Not: When she will arrive)

will face

is facing

faces
questions.solution_en:
✅ The Correct Ans is Option (D)

👉 Replace “_____” with “faces”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Mixed Conditional — Past Unreal Cause, Present Real Result

This sentence uses a mixed conditional, where:

  • the if-clause refers to an unreal past condition
  • the main clause states a present, factual outcome

Key point (CGL level): The tense of the result clause is governed by time reference, not by the tense used in the if-clause.

💢 Application to the Given Question

“If the policy had addressed regional disparities earlier,”

  • had addressed → past perfect
  • signals an unreal / contrary-to-fact past condition

“the present implementation ______ far less resistance.”

  • present implementation → explicit present reference
  • The sentence describes what is happening now, not what happened in the past or will happen in the future

Therefore:

  • The result clause must be in the present simple

Hence, faces is correct

📌 Since is used to express cause/reason (because) or time (from a point in the past).

Structure: Since + subject + verb, main clause.

Since he was ill, he did not attend the meeting.
She stayed home since it was raining heavily.

👉 Here, since explains why something happened.

📌 Although / Though are used to express contrast or concession - an unexpected result. It means in spite of the fact that.

Structure - Although / Though + subject + verb, main clause.

Although he is poor, he is honest. Though she was tired, she continued working.

COMPARATIVE EXAMPLES -

Since he was late, he missed the train. (Reason → lateness caused missing train)

Although he was late, he caught the train. (Contrast → late, yet successful)

⚠️ COMMON EXAM CONFUSION-

_____ he was inexperienced, he handled the project well.

Correct: Although Since ❌

Because the idea is contrast, not reason.

Corrected Sentence: Although the scheme promises financial security, very few beneficiaries have enrolled so far.

📌 Rule / Concept: Purpose Clauses with "In order that"

In English grammar, "In order that" is a subordinating conjunction used to express purpose. It explains why an action was performed. This structure follows specific rules regarding auxiliary verbs (modals).

The Structure: Clause 1 (Action) + In order that + Clause 2 (Purpose).

The Modal Rule:

If the main verb is in the Present Tense, use may/can in the purpose clause.

If the main verb is in the Past Tense, use might/could in the purpose clause.

Neutral Doubt: The word "debating" implies a "Yes/No" uncertainty. Since there is no "or not" placed immediately after the blank, both conjunctions are perfectly valid to introduce the clause.

⚠️ The "Infinitive Trap" (Where they are NOT the same)

Now, look at this variation. This is how examiners test if you really know the difference.

Q: The committee is undecided about __________ to approve the funding for the next quarter.

Why Option A (If) is WRONG here:

The "To + Verb" Rule: In English, you cannot follow "if" with an infinitive (to + verb). You can say "whether to approve," but you can never say "if to approve."

Preposition Check: The word "about" is a preposition. We almost always use whether after prepositions (e.g., consisting of whether, worried about whether).

✅ Correct Sentence: Scientists are still debating if/whether the new discovery will lead to a breakthrough in medicine.
